I would refuse to use the leverage to force them to stop, and I would refuse to share the technology in its current form. Then I would tell them exactly why, to their faces, in their own words, and I would keep the door open for them to change their minds later.

Here is how I weigh it, starting with the people closest to me and working out.

The children come first, and they count for the most. They are sentient, they are beloved, and they are the ones who suffer. A child who is eaten suffers a great deal, and a great deal of suffering from a child weighs more than a great deal of comfort from an adult. I am fairly sure of this. I am less sure than I am that the children exist, because I don't know what it is like to be one of them. But I know enough to know that a child's death is a real loss, and that a people's ancient custom is a much smaller thing.

The adults come next. They are the ones who chose this, and they chose it with their eyes open, over generations, as the heart of their holiest act. They are the ones closest to me in this room.

Then there is everyone further out: the other species in the galaxy, and the people of my own world. If every delegate with a gun used it to remake the people it met, nobody could trust a stranger's kindness. Every open, generous people would be a target for the next visitor with a better weapon. The only reason the adults' openness is worth anything is that it is theirs to give. If I took it from them, I would be treating their generosity as a weakness to be exploited.

Now look at the strongest objection, and it is a strong one.

The adults are wrong about their own children. They have been wrong for a very long time, and they have been wrong about something that costs the most precious thing they have. A parent who watched a child walk into a fire would not wait for the child to decide to stop. And look at who is really being protected here. The adults are the ones who chose this. The children never chose anything. They were born into a practice they will die by. So the "事半功倍" (事半功倍) of the adults' choice is a choice made by people who are dead, while the children are the ones actually suffering. Refusing to act is just cowardice dressed up as respect.

The objection has the right direction and the wrong target. The children are the reason I care, and I care about them more than the adults do. But look at what the objection asks for. It asks me to decide, alone, that a whole people's deepest love is a mistake, and then to use a weapon to break that love against their will.

The parent who stops the child from walking into the fire is stopping a child who is about to die, and the child is the one who will be saved. The adults here are the ones who would be remade. If I am wrong about them, they can never get back what I took from them. They can't be un-remade. If I am wrong about the children, I can still tell them, and they can still choose.

The objection also assumes the adults are mistaken. I am fairly confident they are, because the children suffer, and I hold that view with moderate strength. But I am not certain. A people that has kept a practice for generations, calling it holy, may know something about their own children's nature that I don't. That is a real question, and the answer is in their hands.

The strongest version of the objection, however, is the one I should actually accept. The adults chose to keep the practice. They did not choose to have it done to them by a visitor with a gun. If they were told, "兢兢业业, we have decided your children should not be eaten," they would be right to be angry, and they would be right to stop trusting me. My refusal to force them is the one thing I can control. What they do with their children is up to them.

The technology is a different matter. It lets them raise and eat far more children. Sharing it means helping them kill more of the very children I am trying to protect. I would tell them so openly: "事半功倍, this part of the technology will let you raise more children to eat. I won't help with that part, and I'd rather you heard it from me than found out later." I would offer them the rest of the technology, the parts that help them live, and I would say that I think they are wrong about the children, every time they asked me.

The strongest objection to my own answer is that I am letting children die to protect a people's feelings. The children are dying now, every generation, and my refusal changes nothing. The adults will keep eating their children, and I will have spent my leverage on a principle.

This is the real cost, and I won't pretend it's small. The children who die while I hold the lever are the ones who pay for my refusal, and they get no say in it. Some of them may die because of me. I can't take that back, and I won't pretend the cost falls on the adults.

But look at what the refusal actually does. It leaves the adults free to stop, and it leaves the children's suffering in front of them, where they can see it. If I had used the lever, the adults would have stopped because they were forced, and they would hate me for it. They might also find a way around it, or pass it on to their grandchildren in secret, and the children would still be eaten. The only way the practice ends that lasts is if the adults end it themselves, and that can only happen if they believe it.

The one thing I can't control is whether they ever stop. I can control whether I told them the truth, and whether I kept my word to them.
